qs.q: You are driving a route-service bus and intend to make a U-turn. What must you do in this situation?
o: Make the manoeuvre first, because route-service buses have priority when making U-turns at intersections.
Yield the right of way to the passenger car.
qs.x: A route bus has no priority when making a U-turn and must yield to the approaching passenger car.

qs.q: When approaching a stationary vehicle with a flashing red beacon switched on, drivers of public transport vehicles travelling in the same direction must:
o: Stop and proceed only after receiving permission.
Reduce speed so that they can stop immediately if necessary.
Continue driving because they are operating on a designated route.
qs.x: Approaching a stationary vehicle with a flashing red beacon, public transport drivers must stop and continue only with permission.

qs.q: When a vehicle approaches with a flashing blue beacon and a special audible warning signal switched on, drivers of public transport vehicles must:
o: Continue driving because they are operating on a designated route.
Yield the right of way to ensure the vehicle can pass without obstruction.
Reduce speed and yield the right of way to ensure the vehicle can pass without obstruction.
qs.x: Public transport drivers must give way to a vehicle with a blue beacon and siren; being on a route gives no priority.

qs.q: Drivers of public transport vehicles may use the horn:
o: To gain priority over other road users.
In built-up areas, to warn other drivers of their intention to overtake.
When necessary to prevent a road traffic accident.
In all of the above cases.
qs.x: The horn may be used when needed to prevent a road traffic accident, not to gain priority.

qs.q: When a bus is travelling on a designated route along an unlit section of road during the hours of darkness, which headlights must be switched on?
qs.x: At night on an unlit road section a bus must have either main or dipped beam switched on.

qs.q: During daylight hours, must dipped-beam headlights be switched on for public transport vehicles travelling against the main flow of traffic in a specially designated lane?
qs.x: Public transport in a contraflow lane must use dipped beam even in daylight.

qs.q: In which case do the traffic rules not require a warning signal to be given?
o: When stopping at the edge of the carriageway.
Before a bend in the road within the area of effect of a “Dangerous Bend” sign.
Before changing to an adjacent traffic lane.
qs.x: Following a curve under a Dangerous Turn sign is not a maneuver, so no signal is required.

qs.q: When must a warning signal be given before changing lanes?
o: In good time before starting the manoeuvre.
qs.x: The signal before changing lanes is given in advance, before the maneuver starts, so others can react.

qs.q: When must a warning signal be given when performing a manoeuvre?
o: Before changing the direction of travel.
While changing the direction of travel.
In good time before changing the direction of travel.
qs.x: A warning signal is given in advance, before changing direction.

qs.q: When must a driver give a warning signal before stopping?
o: If another vehicle is travelling behind them.
qs.x: You must signal before stopping in all cases, whether or not another vehicle is behind you.

qs.q: In the event of a compulsory stop on a railway level crossing, what general alarm signal must the driver give using repeated audible signals?
o: Three long signals and one short signal.
One long signal and three short signals.
One long signal and two short signals.
qs.x: When forced to stop on a crossing, the general alarm is one long and three short horn signals.

qs.q: If the direction indicators are missing or defective, when must the warning signal given by hand be discontinued?
qs.x: The hand signal ends right before the maneuver begins so the driver controls the wheel.

qs.q: Which sequence of audible signals constitutes the general alarm signal given at a railway level crossing?
o: Two long signals and two short signals.
One long signal and three short signals.
Three long signals and three short signals.
Three long signals and one short signal.
qs.x: The general alarm at a crossing is one long and three short horn blasts.

qs.q: In which picture is the driver signalling a left turn?
qs.x: In image 1 the red car's driver holds the left arm straight out to the side, the left-turn signal.

qs.q: When approaching a stationary vehicle with a flashing red beacon switched on, drivers travelling in that direction must:
o: Stop and proceed only after receiving permission.
Reduce speed so that they can stop immediately if necessary.
qs.x: At a flashing red beacon drivers must stop and proceed only with permission.

qs.q: For what purpose are flashing amber or yellow beacons fitted to vehicles?
o: To gain priority over other road users.
To warn other road users of a hazard.
qs.x: Orange or yellow flashing beacons warn of danger and give no priority.

qs.q: When a vehicle approaches with a flashing blue beacon and a special audible warning signal switched on, drivers must:
o: Yield the right of way to allow that vehicle to pass without obstruction.
Reduce speed and yield the right of way to allow that vehicle to pass without obstruction.
qs.x: Yield to a vehicle with a blue beacon and siren to let it pass unobstructed.

qs.q: The blue passenger car will pass through the intersection:
o: First, simultaneously with the red passenger car.
Second, simultaneously with the red passenger car.
Third, simultaneously with the red passenger car.
qs.x: The emergency vehicle goes first, then the green car, and the blue and red cars from the minor road go last, together.

qs.q: When a vehicle approaches with flashing blue and red beacons and a special audible warning signal activated, drivers must:
o: Yield the right of way to allow that vehicle to pass without obstruction.
Reduce speed and yield the right of way to allow that vehicle and the vehicles it is escorting to pass without obstruction.
qs.x: For a vehicle with blue-and-red beacons and siren, slow down and give way to it and the vehicles it escorts.

qs.q: Does a flashing amber (orange) beacon activated on a vehicle give it priority over other road users?
qs.x: A yellow or orange flashing beacon only warns and gives no right-of-way.

qs.q: A driver of a vehicle with flashing white beacons activated uses a special audible warning signal in order to:
o: Obtain priority over other road users.
Attract the attention of police officers and other persons.
qs.x: With white flashing beacons the siren only attracts the attention of police and others; it gives no priority.

qs.q: A driver of a vehicle equipped with a flashing blue beacon has priority over other road users if the driver:
o: Uses a special audible warning signal.
Activates both the flashing blue beacon and the special audible warning signal.
qs.x: Priority exists only when both the blue beacon and the special siren are on together.

qs.q: Within what distance before a railway level crossing is overtaking prohibited?
qs.x: Passing is prohibited within 100 m before a railroad crossing.

qs.q: Is overtaking permitted at an intersection when travelling on a road that has priority over the intersecting road?
qs.x: Passing at an intersection is prohibited even when on the priority road.

qs.q: Overtaking is prohibited:
o: Within 150 m before railway level crossings.
qs.x: Passing is banned at intersections; before railroad crossings the ban is 100 m, not 150 m.

qs.q: Overtaking is prohibited:
qs.x: Passing is prohibited at both controlled and uncontrolled intersections.

qs.q: Is overtaking the bus permitted at the location shown?
qs.x: The crossing warning signs show the crossing is still more than 100 m away, so passing is allowed.

qs.q: Overtaking of vehicles means:
o: Passing one or more moving vehicles by leaving the lane occupied and entering a lane intended for oncoming traffic.
Passing one or more moving vehicles by leaving the lane occupied.
qs.x: Passing is getting ahead of one or more moving vehicles by leaving your lane; entering the oncoming lane is not required.

qs.q: During the hours of darkness and in conditions of reduced visibility, regardless of road lighting, moving motor vehicles must have switched on:
qs.x: At night or in poor visibility either high or low beam may be used, depending on the situation.

qs.q: What must a driver do if dazzled by the headlights of an oncoming vehicle?
o: Switch from main-beam to dipped-beam headlights, if the main beam is on.
Switch on the hazard warning lights and, without changing lanes, reduce speed and stop if necessary.
Sound one long and three short audible warning signals.
Sound one short and three long audible warning signals.
qs.x: When dazzled, switch on the hazard lights and, without changing lanes, slow down and stop if necessary.

qs.q: Audible warning signals may be used only:
o: In built-up areas, to warn other drivers of the intention to overtake.
When necessary to prevent a road traffic accident.
qs.x: The horn may be used only when needed to prevent an accident.

qs.q: When a motor vehicle is travelling on an unlit road during the hours of darkness, the following must be switched on:
qs.x: On unlit roads at night either high or low beam is allowed, high beam when there is no oncoming traffic.

qs.q: Rear fog lights may be used:
o: When travelling in a convoy during the hours of darkness.
Only in conditions of reduced visibility.
When unloading a vehicle during the hours of darkness.
qs.x: Rear fog lights may be used only in poor visibility such as fog or heavy rain.

qs.q: At what minimum distance from an oncoming vehicle must main-beam headlights be switched to dipped beam?
qs.x: High beams must be switched to low at least 150 m from an oncoming vehicle.

qs.q: At what distance before the beginning of a hazardous road section is this warning sign installed in built-up areas?
qs.x: In populated areas the Children warning sign is placed 50 to 100 m before the hazard.

qs.q: Where is it permitted to cross railway tracks?
o: At locations where visibility in both directions is at least 1,000 m.
At any suitable location chosen at the driver’s discretion.
Only at designated railway level crossings.
At least 1,000 m from railway stations.
qs.x: Railway tracks may be crossed only at designated railway level crossings.

qs.q: What must a driver observe when approaching a railway level crossing?
o: The position of the barrier and traffic light signals.
The requirements of road signs and road markings.
The instructions of the level crossing attendant.
qs.x: Approaching a crossing the driver must follow all of them: barrier, signals, signs, markings and the attendant.

qs.q: Are pedestrians permitted to use a road marked with the “Motorway” sign?
o: Permitted outside built-up areas when walking against the flow of traffic.
Permitted outside built-up areas when walking in the same direction as traffic.
qs.x: Pedestrians are completely prohibited on a road marked as a freeway.

qs.q: Travel on motorways by vehicles whose maximum speed, due to their design characteristics or technical condition, does not exceed 40 km/h is:
o: Permitted only in the rightmost lane.
Permitted if there is no “Minimum Speed Limit” sign.
qs.x: Vehicles that cannot exceed 40 km/h are prohibited from freeways.

qs.q: Hazard warning lights must be switched on:
o: In the event of a road traffic accident.
In the event of a compulsory stop where stopping is prohibited.
qs.x: Hazard lights are used both after an accident and for a forced stop where stopping is prohibited.

qs.q: Hazard warning lights must be switched on:
o: In the event of a road traffic accident.
During towing, on the towed motor vehicle.
In the event of a compulsory stop where stopping is prohibited.
qs.x: Hazard lights are required in all listed cases: accident, towed vehicle and forced stop in a prohibited place.

qs.q: At what distance from the vehicle must the warning triangle be placed?
o: At least 15 m in built-up areas and at least 30 m outside built-up areas.
At least 10 m in built-up areas and at least 20 m outside built-up areas.
At least 5 m in built-up areas and at least 10 m outside built-up areas.
qs.x: The warning triangle goes at least 15 m behind the vehicle in towns and at least 30 m outside them.

qs.q: Hazard warning lights must be switched on:
o: If the driver is dazzled by headlights.
During towing, on the towed motor vehicle.
qs.x: Hazard lights are used both when dazzled and on a towed motor vehicle.

qs.q: Hazard warning lights must be switched on:
o: In the event of a road traffic accident.
During towing, on the towed motor vehicle.
qs.x: Hazard lights are used both after an accident and on a towed motor vehicle.

qs.q: In areas whose entrances and exits are marked with the “Residential Zone” and “End of Residential Zone” road signs, which of the following is not prohibited?
qs.x: In a residential zone pedestrians may walk on the roadway, while through traffic and driving instruction are prohibited.

qs.q: An intersection is considered controlled if the order of passage is determined by:
o: Signals given by a traffic controller only.
qs.x: An intersection is controlled if priority is set by traffic lights or by a traffic controller.

qs.q: Does a paved section immediately before an intersection make an unpaved dirt road equal in priority to the intersecting road?
qs.x: A short paved stretch before the junction does not make the dirt road equal to the crossing road; it stays minor.

qs.q: Which picture shows the permitted directions of travel?
o: The pictures in the middle and on the right.
qs.x: The right image shows only left, straight and right arrows, while the left and middle ones include the prohibited U-turn.

qs.q: If traffic light signals conflict with the requirements of priority signs, drivers must follow:
qs.x: Traffic signals override priority signs when the two conflict.

qs.q: May a driver continue driving when the traffic light changes to yellow or a traffic controller raises an arm?
o: Permitted if the driver cannot stop without sudden braking.
qs.x: On yellow or a raised controller's arm you may continue only if you cannot stop without sudden braking.

qs.q: A traffic controller uses a whistle:
o: Only when requiring a vehicle to stop.
To attract the attention of road users.
qs.x: A controller's whistle is meant to draw road users' attention.

qs.q: In which case is a bus driver not required by the traffic rules to give a warning signal?
o: When stopping at the edge of the carriageway.
Before a bend on a road section marked with a “Dangerous Bend” sign.
Before changing to an adjacent traffic lane.
qs.x: A warning signal is not required before a bend marked with a 'Dangerous Bend' sign, unlike before changing lanes.

qs.q: Before changing lanes, a bus driver must give a warning signal:
o: In good time before starting the manoeuvre.
Not at all if the bus is operating on a regular route.
qs.x: The signal must be given in good time before the manoeuvre starts, whether or not the bus is on a route.

qs.q: In the event of a compulsory stop at a railway level crossing, what general alarm signal must a bus driver give using repeated audible signals?
o: Three long signals and one short signal.
One long signal and three short signals.
One long signal and two short signals.
Two long signals and two short signals.
qs.x: The general alarm signal at a stalled level crossing is one long and three short blasts, repeated.

qs.q: Is the driver of an intercity bus permitted to overtake a motorcycle travelling at 70 km/h?
qs.x: The bus is at an intersection where overtaking is prohibited, whatever the motorcycle's speed.

qs.q: Is it permitted to give a hand warning signal to travel along the indicated path?
o: Permitted if the direction indicator is defective.
Permitted during daylight hours if the direction indicator is defective.
qs.x: A hand signal is allowed when the turn signal is faulty, like the driver in the picture with the arm out.

qs.q: Must a driver activate the direction indicator before moving off in a residential zone?
o: Yes, if other vehicles are present.
qs.x: Signaling before moving off in a residential zone is mandatory, as before any maneuver.

qs.q: To obtain priority over other road users, the driver of a patrol service vehicle must activate:
o: The flashing blue and red beacons.
The flashing blue beacon and the special audible warning signal.
qs.x: A patrol car gets priority only with the blue beacon and special siren on together.

qs.q: Must a bus driver yield the right of way to an ambulance if its flashing blue beacon and special audible warning signal are not activated?
o: No, the driver is not required to yield.
qs.x: An ambulance without its blue beacon and siren has no priority, so the bus need not yield.

qs.q: Overtaking is prohibited:
o: At railway level crossings and within 100 m before them.
At railway level crossings and within 150 m before them.
At railway level crossings and within 250 m before them.
qs.x: Overtaking is prohibited on railway crossings and within 100 m before them.

qs.q: What does the hand signal given by the driver of the passenger car indicate?
o: The driver is continuing straight ahead.
qs.x: The driver's raised hand signals braking.

qs.q: Hazard warning lights must be switched on:
o: In the event of a road traffic accident.
When travelling as part of an organised convoy.
qs.x: Hazard lights are for a traffic accident, not for entering a tunnel or driving in a convoy.

qs.q: What does the hand signal given by the motorcycle rider indicate?
o: The rider is continuing to the left or making a U-turn.
The rider is continuing straight ahead or turning right.
qs.x: The motorcyclist's arm held straight out to the left signals a left turn or U-turn.

qs.q: What does the hand signal given by the driver of the passenger car indicate?
o: The driver is continuing straight ahead.
The driver is braking to yield the right of way to the motorcycle.
qs.x: The driver's left arm out with the forearm bent up signals a right turn.

qs.q: What does the hand signal given by the driver of the passenger car indicate?
o: The driver intends to turn left or make a U-turn.
The driver is braking to yield the right of way to the truck.
qs.x: An arm held straight out to the left signals intent to turn left or make a U-turn.

qs.q: Is the driver required to activate the direction indicator in this situation?
o: Yes, the driver is required to do so.
No, the driver is not required to do so.
qs.x: The picture shows a right turn at a mandatory right-turn sign, and the turn signal must be on before the maneuver.

qs.q: When transporting organised groups of children during daylight hours, which lights must be switched on on the bus?
qs.x: When carrying organised groups of children by day the bus must have dipped-beam headlights on.

qs.q: Is it permitted to enter the railway level crossing in this situation?
qs.x: The crossing worker holds out a red flag, which forbids entering the crossing.

qs.q: Is it permitted to enter the railway level crossing in this situation?
o: Permitted if no train is approaching.
Permitted if the barrier is open.
qs.x: The red signal is lit and the barrier is lowering, so entering is prohibited even if no train is seen.

qs.q: What should the driver do in this situation?
o: If no train is approaching, drive around the barrier and continue.
Stop and wait for the barrier to open.
qs.x: The barrier is down, so stop and wait for it to open; going around it is forbidden.

qs.q: Is it permitted to cross the railway level crossing in this situation?
o: Permitted if no train is approaching.
qs.x: The truck ahead is stopped with brake lights beyond the tracks, so entering is prohibited because you could get stuck on the crossing.

qs.q: Is it permitted to cross the railway level crossing in this situation?
o: Permitted if no train is approaching.
Permitted because the level crossing attendant is preventing an oncoming vehicle from crossing.
qs.x: The attendant holding a red flag forbids crossing, and the signal applies to everyone, not only the oncoming car.

qs.q: Where may overtaking be started in this situation?
o: After passing the railway level crossing.
100 m after passing the railway level crossing.
qs.x: Passing may begin only after the crossing, since it is banned on and before it.

qs.q: Is overtaking permitted in this situation?
o: Permitted because there is no oncoming vehicle.
Permitted if the horse-drawn cart is travelling at less than 30 km/h.
qs.x: Passing is prohibited in this situation; neither the cart's slow speed nor the lack of oncoming traffic permits it.

qs.q: Is overtaking a motorcycle permitted?
qs.x: Passing the motorcycle is prohibited because an intersection with side roads lies ahead, and passing at intersections is banned.

qs.q: Under what conditions is overtaking using the lane for oncoming traffic permitted on a road with one lane in each direction?
o: Only when the oncoming lane is clear for a sufficient distance.
Only when no vehicle is overtaking us.
qs.x: Overtaking in the oncoming lane requires both a sufficiently clear lane ahead and that nobody is overtaking you.

qs.q: Is overtaking permitted in the situation shown?
o: Yes, provided the manoeuvre can be completed within the visible distance.
qs.x: The markings are dashed, the lane is clear with good visibility, and the 7% descent sign is no restriction, so passing is allowed.

qs.q: Is overtaking the truck permitted?
o: Yes, provided the overtaking manoeuvre is completed before the intersection.
qs.x: Passing at an intersection is prohibited, so it is allowed only if it is completed before reaching the intersection.

qs.q: What is required of the driver of a vehicle being overtaken?
o: The driver must yield the right of way to the overtaking vehicle.
The driver must not obstruct the overtaking vehicle by increasing speed or taking any other action.
qs.x: The driver being overtaken must not hinder the overtaking by speeding up or any other action.

qs.q: Is overtaking permitted in this situation?
o: Yes, if the truck is travelling at less than 30 km/h.
qs.x: The picture shows a No Passing sign, which applies regardless of the truck's speed.

qs.q: Overtaking at a pedestrian crossing is:
o: Prohibited only when pedestrians are present.
qs.x: Overtaking at a pedestrian crossing is prohibited whether or not pedestrians are present.

qs.q: What does this road sign indicate?
o: A rest area along a 500-metre section of road.
qs.x: The sign marks a rest area, and the plate below shows that it is 500 m ahead.

qs.q: In the situation shown, the driver:
o: Must activate the turn indicator if a vehicle is approaching from behind.
Is not required to activate the turn indicator.
qs.x: You are just following the bend of the road in your lane, so there is no maneuver and no signal is required.

qs.q: By raising one arm vertically, the driver signals an intention to:
qs.x: The raised arm of the driver ahead signals slowing down or stopping.

qs.q: Does giving a signal confer priority over other road users?
qs.x: Signalling gives no priority; it only informs others of your intention.

qs.q: When turning right while following a priority road, signalling is:
o: Mandatory only during the hours of darkness.
qs.x: A turn is a maneuver, so signaling a right turn is required at any time of day, even on the priority road.

qs.q: What is the motorcycle rider signalling?
o: An intention to continue straight ahead.
An intention to slow down to yield the right of way to the passenger car.
qs.x: The motorcyclist's raised arm signals slowing down, here to yield to the passenger car approaching from the right.

qs.q: When turning left in this situation, signalling is:
qs.x: Signalling before a left turn is always mandatory, even when the main road itself bends left.

qs.q: Which turn indicator must be activated when making a U-turn at this intersection?
qs.x: When leaving a roundabout, the right turn signal is switched on.

qs.q: Are you required to signal with a turn indicator in the situation shown?
o: Yes, if there is a driver travelling in the right-hand lane.
qs.x: Changing lanes is a maneuver, so signaling is required regardless of other traffic.

qs.q: What is the motorcycle rider signalling?
o: An intention to continue straight ahead.
An intention to turn left or make a U-turn.
qs.x: An arm extended sideways to the left signals a left turn or U-turn.

qs.q: A manoeuvre signal given using a turn indicator must be cancelled:
qs.x: The signal is canceled immediately after the maneuver is completed.

qs.q: In the situation shown, using a turn indicator is:
qs.x: Signalling with the indicator is mandatory when changing lanes to go around an obstacle such as the goats.

qs.q: Which driver is signalling a right turn?
o: Only the driver on the right.
Only the driver on the left.
qs.x: An arm bent upward on the left and an arm extended to the right both signal a right turn.

qs.q: When manoeuvring in parking areas or at petrol stations, you:
o: Are not required to use the turn indicators.
qs.x: Using the turn indicator when manoeuvring is mandatory in parking areas and at petrol stations too.

qs.q: In this situation, what might the driver’s outstretched arm indicate?
o: A signal that the driver intends to move off.
A signal indicating an intention to stop.
qs.x: An arm out of a car stopped at the roadside signals the intention to pull out onto the road.

qs.q: Which turn indicator signals must you give when making a U-turn along the indicated path?
qs.x: On this path you first signal right (moving to the edge) and then left for the U-turn itself.

qs.q: If you intend to stop immediately after an intersection, when should you activate the right turn indicator to avoid confusing other road users?
qs.x: Signaling right only after entering the intersection avoids suggesting that you will turn at the intersection itself.

qs.q: When a driver using special audible and light signals is emerging from an adjacent area, we:
o: Are not required to yield the right of way.
Must yield the right of way.
qs.x: The police car with its special light and sound signals has priority, so we must yield.

qs.q: When proceeding straight through the intersection, must we yield the right of way to the driver of the truck with flashing amber beacons activated?
qs.x: A flashing yellow beacon gives no priority, it only warns, so you need not yield to that truck.

qs.q: In this situation, you:
o: Will proceed through the intersection first.
Must yield the right of way to the driver approaching from the left.
qs.x: The police car approaching from the left has its special signals on, so we must yield to it.

qs.q: We must yield the right of way to:
o: The driver of the police vehicle.
qs.x: We are on the priority road, so we yield only to the police car using its special signals.

qs.q: When turning left, you:
o: Will proceed through the intersection first.
Will yield the right of way only to the driver of the police vehicle.
Will yield the right of way to all drivers.
qs.x: Turning left, we yield to the oncoming car and the police car with special signals, so to everyone.

qs.q: In which of the following cases must a bus driver switch on the hazard warning lights?
o: When picking up or setting down children during the organised transport of a group of children.
In the event of a road traffic accident.
When transporting groups of children outside built-up areas.
qs.x: Hazard lights are required when children board or alight and at an accident scene, not merely for driving outside built-up areas.

qs.q: In which case must a bus driver switch on the hazard warning lights?
o: When travelling against the general flow of traffic in a lane specially reserved for public transport vehicles.
When making a compulsory stop in a place where stopping is prohibited.
qs.x: Hazard lights are required for a forced stop where stopping is banned; the contraflow lane requires dipped beam instead.

qs.q: A bus driver switches on the hazard warning lights when:
o: It is necessary to warn other road users of a danger.
qs.x: Hazard lights are for warning others of danger; reversing is covered by the reversing lights.

qs.q: Is a bus driver permitted to stop within the area of effect of a “No Stopping” sign by switching on the hazard warning lights?
o: Only public transport buses may do so to pick up or set down passengers.
Only in the event of a compulsory stop.
qs.x: Hazard lights justify stopping under a No Stopping sign only in the case of a forced stop.

qs.q: When carrying out an urgent official duty, may drivers of vehicles using a blue flashing beacon and a special audible warning signal disregard signals given by a traffic controller?
qs.x: Vehicles with blue beacon and siren must still obey the traffic controller's signals.

qs.q: When may drivers of vehicles using a blue flashing beacon and a special audible warning signal exercise priority?
o: Immediately after switching on the special audible warning signal, regardless of the actions of other drivers.
Only after ensuring that other road users are yielding the right of way.
Only when no public transport vehicles are present.
qs.x: A driver with special signals may use priority only after making sure others are yielding.

qs.q: Do vehicles merely following a vehicle using blue and red flashing beacons and a special audible warning signal, without being escorted by it, have priority?
o: No, priority applies only to drivers of vehicles using the special signals and to vehicles they are escorting.
Yes, but only if the following vehicle has switched on its hazard warning lights.
qs.x: Only the vehicles with special signals and those they escort have priority, not vehicles simply following.

qs.q: May drivers of vehicles using yellow or orange flashing beacons disregard the requirement of this sign, provided that road safety is ensured?
qs.x: A yellow or orange beacon does not exempt a driver from the sign (no overtaking); only vehicles with blue beacon and siren have that right.

qs.q: Yellow or orange flashing beacons must be switched on on vehicles engaged in:
o: Road construction, repair, maintenance or cleaning operations.
Agricultural work within a built-up area.
Loading and transporting broken-down, accident-damaged or other vehicles.
qs.x: Yellow or orange beacons are required for road works and for loading and carrying broken-down vehicles.

qs.q: Drivers of vehicles equipped with white flashing beacons may switch them on:
o: To obtain priority when passing through intersections.
Together with a special audible warning signal, only in the event of an attack on those vehicles.
At their discretion, whenever they consider it appropriate.
qs.x: White flashing beacons are used with the siren only if those vehicles are attacked.

qs.q: What is a driver of a vehicle carrying out an urgent official duty with a blue flashing beacon and a special audible warning signal prohibited from doing?
o: Turning while a traffic light displays a prohibitory signal.
Failing to signal with the appropriate turn indicator before performing a manoeuvre.
Exceeding the prescribed maximum permitted speed.
qs.x: Special-signal drivers may depart from several rules, but not from signalling a manoeuvre with the indicator.

qs.q: What is a driver of a vehicle carrying out an urgent official duty with a blue flashing beacon and a special audible warning signal prohibited from doing?
o: Crossing a continuous longitudinal road marking.
Travelling in the opposite direction on a one-way road.
Failing to signal with the appropriate turn indicator before performing a manoeuvre.
qs.x: A special-signal driver may cross a continuous line, but may not skip the turn-indicator signal before a manoeuvre.

qs.q: Must a bus driver use the appropriate turn indicator before moving off if there are no other vehicles on the road at that moment?
o: No, if the bus is a public transport vehicle.
qs.x: The turn signal before moving off is mandatory regardless of whether other vehicles are around.

qs.q: When must a bus driver switch on the turn indicator before performing a manoeuvre?
o: In good time before beginning the manoeuvre.
One to two seconds after beginning the manoeuvre.
qs.x: The turn indicator must be switched on in good time before the manoeuvre begins.

qs.q: Must a bus driver switch on the turn indicator if the bus remains in the same lane but the road changes direction at that point?
o: Yes, because the direction of travel of the bus changes.
Only if the road bends by more than 90 degrees.
qs.x: If the bus stays in its lane and only the road bends, no turn indicator is required.

qs.q: Must a bus driver use a turn indicator when reversing?
o: No, because the hazard warning lights must be switched on when reversing.
No, because the white reversing lights are sufficient to warn other drivers.
qs.x: Turn indicators are required when reversing as for any manoeuvre; reversing lights or hazards do not replace them.

qs.q: Must a bus driver use a turn indicator when changing direction in courtyards or other adjoining areas?
o: No, because courtyards are not considered public roads.
No, if no other vehicles are present in the courtyard at that moment.
Yes, because the rules on manoeuvring apply on all types of roads and in all such areas.
qs.x: The rules on signalling manoeuvres apply on all roads and adjacent areas, courtyards included.

qs.q: When must a bus driver switch off the turn indicator used to signal a lane change for overtaking?
o: Immediately after passing the vehicle being overtaken.
After returning to the lane previously occupied.
qs.x: The indicator is switched off after the manoeuvre is completed.

qs.q: A bus driver is prohibited from overtaking:
o: A vehicle with a blue flashing beacon and a special audible warning signal activated.
A vehicle with a blue flashing beacon activated, even if its special audible warning signal is not activated.
qs.x: Overtaking is banned for a vehicle with both blue beacon and siren on, not for one with only the beacon.

qs.q: A bus driver is prohibited from overtaking vehicles if they:
o: Have an amber or yellow flashing beacon activated.
Have blue and red flashing beacons and a special audible warning signal activated, or are being escorted by such vehicles.
qs.x: Overtaking is banned for vehicles with blue-red beacons and siren or those escorted by them; a yellow beacon does not ban it.

qs.q: In which case is a bus driver prohibited from overtaking?
o: When the vehicle being overtaken has special colour markings.
When overtaking at a railway level crossing or within 100 metres before it.
qs.x: Overtaking is banned at a level crossing and within 100 m before it; special livery on the other vehicle does not matter.

qs.q: When must a bus driver avoid obstructing blind pedestrians signalling their presence with a white cane?
qs.x: Drivers must not hinder blind pedestrians with white canes in all cases, not just at crossings.

qs.q: When must a bus driver avoid obstructing blind pedestrians signalling their presence with a white cane?
o: Only where the 'Blind Pedestrians' supplementary information sign is installed.
qs.x: Blind pedestrians with white canes must not be obstructed in all cases, even without a supplementary sign.

qs.q: Where is a bus permitted to cross railway tracks?
o: At any point where the rails do not obstruct the bus and no train is visible.
Only at railway level crossings, yielding the right of way to trains.
qs.x: Railway tracks may be crossed only at level crossings, giving way to trains.

qs.q: In which case is a railway level crossing attendant's signal considered prohibitory?
o: When the attendant faces the driver and gestures to stop with one hand.
When the attendant faces towards or away from the driver with arms extended to the sides or raised, holding a baton, red lamp or flag.
qs.x: The attendant's signal is prohibitory when they face towards or away from the driver with arms out or raised, or hold a baton, red lamp or flag.

qs.q: Is a bus driver permitted to enter a railway level crossing if the barrier has started to close but the prohibitory traffic signal has not yet come on?
o: Yes, if no approaching train is visible.
Yes, but only for scheduled-service buses.
qs.x: Entering a crossing is prohibited once the barrier starts to close, even if the signal has not yet come on.

qs.q: Is a bus driver permitted to enter a railway level crossing if the red traffic signal is flashing but the barrier is still open?
o: Yes, if no approaching train is visible.
Yes, as long as the barrier has not started to lower.
qs.x: A flashing red crossing signal prohibits entry even though the barrier is still open.

qs.q: Is a bus driver permitted to enter a railway level crossing if traffic congestion has developed beyond it?
o: Yes, but only for scheduled-service buses.
No, if the congestion would force the driver to stop on the crossing.
Yes, if the driver is confident that the crossing can be cleared before a train approaches.
qs.x: Entering is prohibited if a jam beyond the crossing would force the bus to stop on it.

qs.q: Is a bus driver permitted to pass vehicles stopped before a railway level crossing without entering the lane of oncoming traffic?
qs.x: Passing vehicles queued before a crossing is allowed as long as you do not enter the oncoming lane.

qs.q: Is a bus that is towing another vehicle permitted to cross a railway level crossing?
qs.x: There is no ban on a towing bus crossing a level crossing, so it is permitted.

qs.q: Which lights must a bus driver switch on when driving through a tunnel?
o: Position lights, if the tunnel has adequate artificial lighting.
qs.x: In tunnels a bus must have dipped or main beam headlights on.

qs.q: Must a bus driver switch on dipped-beam or main-beam headlights when driving through a tunnel with adequate artificial lighting?
qs.x: Dipped or main beam is mandatory in a tunnel even with adequate artificial lighting.

qs.q: Which lights must be switched on when a bus is driven at night on roads with adequate artificial lighting within built-up areas?
o: Main-beam or dipped-beam headlights, at the driver's discretion.
qs.x: At night on a lit road in a built-up area a bus must use dipped beam.

qs.q: Main-beam headlights must be switched to dipped beam:
o: In built-up areas when the road is illuminated.
Outside built-up areas at a distance of not less than 100 metres from an oncoming vehicle.
qs.x: Main beam must be dipped in a built-up area when the road is lit.

qs.q: Which lights must be switched on when a bus is stopped or parked on an unlit section of road at night?
qs.x: When stopped or parked at night on an unlit section, position lights must be on.

qs.q: Which lights must be switched on when a bus is stopped or parked on a road in conditions of poor visibility?
o: Position lights; dipped-beam headlights and fog lights may also be switched on.
Only main-beam headlights, so that the bus can be seen from a long distance.
qs.x: In poor visibility, position lights are required when stopped or parked; dipped beam and fog lights are optional extras.

qs.q: During daylight hours, dipped-beam headlights must be switched on to make a bus more visible:
o: Only when the bus is being towed by another vehicle because of a mechanical fault.
When carrying organized groups of children.
qs.x: By day dipped beam is required when carrying organised groups of children; being towed does not create that requirement.

qs.q: During daylight hours, dipped-beam headlights must be switched on to make a bus more visible:
o: When travelling in an organized convoy.
Only when travelling on international routes.
qs.x: In an organised convoy by day a bus must have dipped beam on.

qs.q: When is a bus driver permitted to sound the horn in a built-up area?
o: To warn other drivers of the intention to overtake.
When necessary to prevent a road traffic accident.
qs.x: In a built-up area the horn is allowed only to prevent an accident, not to warn of overtaking.

qs.q: During daylight hours, a light signal may be given instead of, or together with, an audible warning to indicate the intention to overtake. What does this signal consist of?
o: Repeatedly switching the headlights from dipped beam to main beam.
Repeatedly switching the headlights on and off.
qs.x: By day the light signal warning of overtaking is the periodic switching of the headlights on and off.

qs.q: At night, a light signal may be given instead of, or together with, an audible warning to indicate the intention to overtake. What does this signal consist of?
o: Repeatedly switching the headlights from dipped beam to main beam.
Repeatedly switching the headlights on and off.
qs.x: At night the overtaking light signal is repeatedly switching from dipped to main beam.

qs.q: Which light signal must be switched on when children board or alight from a bus displaying the 'Transportation of Children' identification sign?
qs.x: Hazard lights must be on while children board or alight from a bus with the Transportation of Children sign.

qs.q: What must a driver do when approaching a stationary bus displaying the 'Transportation of Children' identification sign with its hazard warning lights switched on, while children are boarding or alighting?
o: Stop immediately and wait until the bus switches off its hazard warning lights and starts moving.
Reduce speed and, if necessary, stop to allow children to cross the carriageway without obstruction.
qs.x: Near a stopped children's bus with hazards on, reduce speed and stop if needed so the children can cross freely.

qs.q: For what purpose does a traffic officer use a baton, including one fitted with a red signal or a retroreflective disc?
o: To make the signals more visible.
To indicate the exact location where vehicles must stop.
qs.x: The baton, red signal or reflective disc simply makes the controller's signals more visible.

qs.q: Is it permitted to drive with only the fog lights switched on in conditions of poor visibility?
o: No. Dipped-beam or main-beam headlights must also be switched on.
qs.x: Fog lights alone are not enough; dipped or main beam must be on at the same time.

qs.q: At the scene of a road traffic accident, the driver of a route-service bus must:
o: Switch on the hazard warning lights only.
qs.x: At an accident scene the driver must both switch on the hazard lights and place the warning triangle.

qs.q: When a vehicle with a blue flashing beacon and a special audible signal approaches, drivers of public transport vehicles must:
o: Continue driving because they are operating on scheduled routes.
Stop and proceed only after receiving permission.
Yield the right of way to allow the approaching vehicle to pass without obstruction.
qs.x: Public transport drivers must give way so the vehicle with blue beacon and siren can pass unobstructed.

qs.q: When approaching a stationary vehicle with a red flashing beacon switched on, drivers of public transport vehicles travelling in that direction must:
o: Yield the right of way to allow that vehicle to pass without obstruction.
Stop and proceed only after receiving permission.
Continue driving because they are operating on scheduled routes.
qs.x: Approaching a stationary vehicle with a flashing red beacon, a public transport driver must stop and proceed only with permission.

qs.q: During the hours of darkness, on illuminated sections of road, a bus operating on a scheduled route must have the following lights switched on:
qs.x: On a lit road at night a route bus uses dipped beam only.

qs.q: In built-up areas, drivers of public transport vehicles may use audible warning signals:
o: To gain priority over other road users.
When necessary to prevent a road traffic accident.
To warn other drivers of their intention to overtake.
qs.x: In a built-up area the horn may be used only to prevent a road accident.

qs.q: During daylight hours, which lights must a bus have switched on to indicate that it is travelling in an organised convoy?
qs.x: In an organised convoy by day a bus is marked by dipped-beam headlights.

qs.q: May a bus driver use a headlight signal instead of, or together with, an audible warning signal to warn of an intention to overtake?
qs.x: A light signal may be used instead of, or together with, the horn to warn of overtaking.

qs.q: The hazard warning lights of a bus must be switched on:
o: To gain priority over other vehicles.
On the towing bus during towing.
When it is necessary to warn other road users of danger.
In all of the above cases.
qs.x: Hazard lights are switched on to warn other road users of danger.

qs.q: When approaching a stationary vehicle with blue, or blue and red, flashing beacons switched on, a bus driver must:
o: Stop and continue driving only after receiving permission.
Reduce speed so that the bus can be stopped if necessary.
qs.x: Approaching a stationary vehicle with blue or blue-red beacons, slow down so you can stop if necessary.

qs.q: When approaching a stationary vehicle displaying a red flashing beacon, a bus driver travelling in that direction must:
o: Stop and continue driving only after receiving permission.
qs.x: Approaching a stationary vehicle with a flashing red beacon, the bus driver must stop and continue only with permission.

qs.q: A bus driver must not obstruct blind pedestrians crossing the carriageway:
o: In all of the above cases.
qs.x: Blind pedestrians must not be obstructed either at crossings or elsewhere on the carriageway.

qs.q: A bus driver is prohibited from crossing a railway level crossing if the crossing attendant:
o: Is standing with their chest or back facing the driver.
Gives a signal with a baton, a red light or a flag raised above their head.
In all of the above cases.
qs.x: All the listed positions and signals of the attendant are prohibitory, so crossing is not allowed.

qs.q: When approaching a railway level crossing, a bus driver must comply with:
o: Instructions given by the crossing attendant.
Traffic lights, road signs and markings controlling traffic at the railway level crossing, as well as the position of the barrier.
qs.x: At a level crossing the driver must follow the attendant, signals, signs, markings and barrier position, all together.

qs.q: During daylight hours, public transport vehicles travelling against the main traffic flow in a specially designated lane must have the following lights switched on:
qs.x: Public transport in a contraflow lane must have dipped beam on in daytime.

qs.q: When this sign is displayed, public transport vehicles must have the following lights switched on during daylight hours:
qs.x: The sign shows a with-flow bus lane, which carries no extra daytime lighting requirement.

qs.q: When this sign is displayed, drivers of public transport vehicles must switch on the following lights during daylight hours:
qs.x: The sign shows a contraflow bus lane, where dipped beam is required in daytime.

qs.q: When a bus is stopped or parked on an unlit section of road during the hours of darkness, the following lights must be switched on:
qs.x: When stopped or parked at night on an unlit section, position lights must be on.

qs.q: A bus driver must switch from main-beam to dipped-beam headlights:
o: Whenever necessary to avoid dazzling drivers of oncoming vehicles.
Whenever necessary to avoid dazzling drivers of vehicles travelling in the same direction.
At a distance of not less than 150 metres from oncoming vehicles.
In all of the above cases.
qs.x: Main beam is dipped to avoid dazzling oncoming or same-direction drivers and at 150 m from oncoming vehicles.

qs.q: The bus driver must switch off the left turn indicator:
o: After changing to the left lane.
After returning to the right lane.
qs.x: The left indicator is switched off once the move into the left lane is complete.

qs.q: Which external lights must be switched on when children are boarding or alighting from a vehicle displaying the 'Transporting Children' identification sign?
o: Dipped-beam headlights or front fog lights.
qs.x: On a vehicle with the Transportation of Children sign, hazard lights must be on while children board or alight.

qs.q: When providing first aid to a person with a head injury, you should:
o: Lay the person down with their legs raised.
Lay the person down with their head and upper body raised, in a semi-reclining position.
Lay the person flat in a horizontal position.
qs.x: With a head injury, the person is placed in a semi-reclined position with head and torso raised.

qs.q: Which of the following casualties should receive first aid first following a road traffic accident?
o: A man with a fractured upper arm.
qs.x: An unconscious person is in immediate life-threatening danger (airway risk), so he is helped first.

qs.q: When providing first aid to a casualty with a nosebleed, you should:
o: Lower the casualty's head and pinch the upper part of the nose.
Insert a cotton swab into the casualty's nostril.
Allow the bleeding to stop on its own.
qs.x: For a nosebleed, tilt the head forward and pinch the nose so blood does not run down the throat.

qs.q: While driving, a driver suddenly complains of severe, crushing chest pain and difficulty breathing. What should be done?
o: Suggest that the driver go to the nearest hospital.
Give the driver a glass of water and two valerian tablets.
Stop the vehicle immediately and switch on the hazard warning lights.
Advise the driver to walk a little and get some fresh air.
qs.x: Severe chest pressure and breathlessness may signal a heart emergency, so stop the vehicle immediately and turn on the hazard lights.

qs.q: What first aid should be given to a casualty having a seizure?
o: Hold the casualty down to try to stop the convulsions.
Try to open the casualty’s mouth, hold the tongue and place an object between the teeth.
Try to open the airway by tilting the casualty’s head back.
Do not interfere; allow the convulsions to stop.
qs.x: During a seizure do not restrain the person or put anything in the mouth; let it run its course.

qs.q: What should be done when providing first aid for a burn?
o: Burst any fluid-filled blisters and then apply a tight bandage.
Cool the burn with water, then cover it with a sterile dressing or clean cloth.
qs.x: Cool the burn with water, then cover it with sterile or clean material; never pop blisters or apply oil.

qs.q: Following a road traffic accident, a pedestrian has fallen and injured an arm. There is a large wound (approximately 5 cm long) on the forearm, from which dark-coloured blood is flowing steadily. What should be done to stop the bleeding?
o: Raise the injured arm and apply a pressure dressing.
Apply an alcoholic iodine solution to the wound.
qs.x: Steady dark blood is venous bleeding: apply a pressure bandage and raise the arm.

qs.q: When providing first aid during the first few hours after a closed soft-tissue injury to a limb, you should:
o: Apply a warm compress to the injured area.
Apply a cold compress to the injured area and elevate it.
Apply a cold compress to the injured area and keep it below heart level.
Apply an alcohol compress to the injured area.
qs.x: In the first hours after a closed injury, apply cold and elevate the limb to reduce swelling.

qs.q: A driver has been crouching for a long time while changing a vehicle tyre. On standing up suddenly, the driver holds their head, loses consciousness and falls. What should you do?
o: Try to sit the driver up.
Splash cold water on the driver’s face.
qs.x: For fainting, raise the legs to improve blood flow to the brain.

qs.q: What should you do if you cannot ensure that the scene of an incident is safe?
o: Provide assistance to everyone, but be careful.
Provide assistance to the casualty nearest to you.
Do not approach; immediately call the emergency services and prevent bystanders from approaching the scene.
Do not approach; ask someone else to provide assistance.
qs.x: If the scene cannot be made safe, do not approach, call for help at once and keep bystanders away.

qs.q: You see a person lying on the ground and notice a bone protruding from the lower leg and bleeding. If the scene is safe, what should you do first?
o: Check the casualty’s responsiveness and breathing.
qs.x: Once the scene is safe, first check consciousness and breathing, as they are the most vital.

qs.q: When providing first aid to a casualty with an open fracture of a limb, you should:
o: Cover the wound with a sterile dressing and immobilise the injured limb.
Stop the bleeding by applying direct pressure.
Apply cold compresses to the wound.
qs.x: For an open fracture, cover the wound with a sterile dressing and immobilize the limb.

qs.q: In the event of a chest injury, you should:
o: Seat the casualty, supporting them on the injured side.
Seat the casualty, supporting them on the uninjured side.
qs.x: With a chest injury, seat the person leaning on the injured side to ease breathing.

qs.q: If internal organs protrude through an open abdominal wound, you should:
o: Wash the protruding organs and carefully try to put them back in place.
Cover the protruding organs with a clean, damp cloth and plastic film.
Cut off the protruding organs and bandage the wound.
Do not touch the organs; transport the casualty to hospital in this condition.
qs.x: Do not touch or push back protruding organs; cover them with a clean moist cloth and plastic film.

qs.q: A casualty who is unconscious but breathing should be:
o: Have their mouth opened and tongue pulled out.
Turned onto their side, with the head tilted back.
qs.x: An unconscious but breathing person is turned onto the side with the head tilted back to keep the airway open.

qs.q: In the event of severe bleeding, you should:
o: Only cover the wound with a dressing.
Apply a pressure bandage to the injured area and press on the arterial pressure point.
qs.x: For severe bleeding, apply a pressure bandage and press the artery at its pressure point.

qs.q: In the event of a road traffic accident, what should you do first?
o: Place the casualty in a comfortable position.
Assess the scene and ensure it is safe.
Check the casualty for severe bleeding.
Remove the casualty from the vehicle.
qs.x: At a crash, first assess the scene and make it safe.

qs.q: If a foreign object is embedded in a casualty’s wound, you should:
o: Remove the foreign object from the wound.
Allow the injured area to continue bleeding.
Treat the area around the wound with alcohol.
qs.x: Do not remove a foreign object from a wound; keep it immobilized to avoid worsening bleeding.

qs.q: What is the pulse rate of an adult at rest?
qs.x: A resting adult's pulse is 60–80 beats per minute.

qs.q: What is the breathing rate of an adult at rest?
qs.x: A resting adult breathes 12–18 times per minute.

qs.q: When should a casualty be removed from a vehicle following a road traffic accident?
o: When the casualty has serious injuries.
When the scene is dangerous, for example, if there is a risk of explosion.
When a live electrical cable has fallen onto the vehicle.
qs.x: An injured person is removed from the vehicle only if the scene is dangerous, e.g., explosion risk.

qs.q: When providing first aid for suspected internal abdominal bleeding, you should:
o: Lay the casualty down and apply a cold compress to the injured area.
Place a hot-water bottle on the abdomen.
Apply a pressure bandage to the abdomen.
Give the casualty plenty of fluids.
qs.x: For suspected internal abdominal bleeding, lay the person down and apply cold to the abdomen.

qs.q: You hear a vehicle engine running in your neighbour’s garage. When you open the door, you see your neighbour lying on the ground. What should you do first?
o: Open the doors wide and switch off the engine; if possible, move the casualty away from the scene.
Carefully examine the casualty’s body for injuries.
Place the casualty in the recovery position on their side.
Help the casualty into a semi-sitting position.
qs.x: Exhaust gas in the garage is deadly, so first open the doors, turn off the engine and, if possible, remove the person.

qs.q: After finding an unconscious casualty, what should you do first?
o: Turn the casualty onto their side into the recovery position.
Maintain the casualty’s normal body temperature.
Open the airway and check for breathing.
qs.x: For an unconscious person, first open the airway and check breathing.

qs.q: To check circulation in an injured limb, you press and release a fingernail or toenail below the bandage. Circulation in the limb is impaired if:
o: The nail is slow to turn white when pressed.
The nail is slow to return to pink after pressure is released.
qs.x: If the nail is slow to turn pink again after pressing, circulation is impaired.

qs.q: Your friend, who has diabetes, feels unwell and cannot remember when they last took insulin. What should you do first?
o: Give your friend sugar or a sweet drink.
Suggest that your friend rest for several hours.
Advise your friend to inject insulin.
qs.x: A diabetic's malaise may be low blood sugar, so first give sugar or a sweet drink.

qs.q: Bleeding is most dangerous when:
o: Blood flows steadily from the wound.
qs.x: Spurting blood is arterial bleeding, the most dangerous because of rapid blood loss.

qs.q: A vehicle has struck a utility pole, and an electrical cable has fallen onto an unconscious casualty lying beside the vehicle. When providing assistance, what should you do first?
o: Move the casualty away from the electrical source.
Remove the cable from the casualty using an insulating object.
Look for electrical entry and exit wounds (burns) on the casualty’s body.
qs.x: First remove the hazard: move the wire off the person with an insulating object so the rescuer is not harmed.

qs.q: To protect yourself from infection when providing first aid, you should:
o: Avoid direct contact with the wound and provide assistance only while wearing sterile gloves.
Do not assist casualties who are bleeding.
qs.x: To avoid infection, avoid direct contact with the wound and wear sterile gloves.

qs.q: During an asthma attack, you should:
o: Help the casualty into a semi-sitting position.
Lay the casualty down and raise their legs.
Lay the casualty down with their knees bent.
Lay the casualty down with their head elevated.
qs.x: During an asthma attack a semi-sitting position makes breathing easier.

qs.q: A casualty with an abdominal injury should be:
o: Laid down with their head elevated.
Laid down with their legs raised.
Laid down with their knees bent.
qs.x: With an abdominal injury, lay the person down with knees bent to relax the abdominal muscles.

qs.q: If a casualty faints, you should:
o: Help the casualty into a semi-sitting position.
Lay the casualty down and raise their legs.
Lay the casualty down with their knees bent.
Lay the casualty down with their head elevated.
qs.x: For fainting, lay the person down and raise the legs to improve blood supply to the brain.

qs.q: If a vehicle with a low front end collides with an adult pedestrian who is at least 1.55 m tall, the pedestrian is most likely to sustain injuries to:
qs.x: A low-front car hits an adult's legs, and the person then falls onto the hood, so lower limbs and head are injured.

qs.q: If a vehicle with a low front end collides with a child aged 3–5 years, the child is most likely to sustain injuries to:
qs.x: Because a 3–5 year old is small, a low-front car strikes the pelvis and chest.

qs.q: If an electrical cable has fallen onto a vehicle, you should:
o: Help the occupants get out of the vehicle immediately.
Ask the occupants to remain inside the vehicle until the electrical power has been switched off.
qs.x: If a wire lies on a vehicle, occupants should stay inside until the power is cut, since stepping out risks electrocution.

qs.q: When treating minor wounds, you should:
o: Wash the wound with soap and clean water, then apply a dressing.
Treat the wound with alcohol-containing substances (iodine, vodka, perfume, etc.).
qs.x: Wash a minor wound with soap and clean water and bandage it; alcohol damages tissue.

qs.q: When treating serious wounds, you should:
o: Wash the wound with soap and clean water.
Treat the wound with alcohol-containing substances (iodine, vodka, perfume, etc.).
Stop the bleeding and apply a dressing to the wound.
qs.x: For a serious wound the priority is to stop the bleeding and bandage it.

qs.q: When calling an ambulance following a road traffic accident, what information should be provided to the emergency dispatcher?
o: Identify the nearest landmark to the accident scene. State the number of casualties and their sex and age.
Give the street name and building number nearest to the accident scene. State who was injured in the accident (a pedestrian, driver or passenger) and describe their injuries.

Give the location of the accident (street, building number and nearest landmarks). State the number of casualties, their sex, approximate age, whether they are conscious and breathing, their circulation status, and whether there is severe bleeding, fractures or other injuries. Wait until the dispatcher confirms that the call has been received.
qs.x: When calling an ambulance give the exact location and the number, sex, age and condition of casualties, then wait for the dispatcher's confirmation.

qs.q: What is the most appropriate position for a conscious casualty when a spinal injury is suspected?
o: Lay the casualty on their side.
Lay the casualty on their back on a firm, flat surface; do not move them or change their position unless necessary.
Lay the casualty on their back, place a roll of clothing under their neck and elevate their legs.
qs.x: With a suspected spinal injury, keep a conscious casualty on their back on a firm flat surface and do not move them unnecessarily.

qs.q: How should first aid be provided for frostbite and hypothermia?
o: Rub the affected areas with snow or woollen cloth, then warm them; give an alcoholic drink and move the casualty to a warm place.
Warm and immobilise the affected areas, cover the casualty with warm clothing or a blanket, give a warm drink and move them to a warm place.
Apply ointment to the affected areas, use a warming compress and a hot-water bottle, move the casualty to a warm place and give a warm drink.
qs.x: For frostbite, gently warm and immobilize the affected parts, cover the person and give warm drinks; no rubbing or alcohol.

qs.q: What first aid should be provided for a head injury involving a wound to the scalp?
o: Control the bleeding by applying direct pressure to the wound and apply a pressure dressing. If the casualty loses consciousness, place them in the recovery position. If possible, apply a cold compress to the injured part of the head.

Immobilise the cervical spine using an improvised splint (collar). Apply a sterile cotton swab to the wound and lay the casualty on their back with their legs elevated. If possible, apply a cold compress to the head.
Do not apply a cervical splint. Cover the wound with medical adhesive tape and lay the casualty on their side.
qs.x: For a scalp wound, control bleeding with direct pressure and a pressure dressing, use the recovery position if unconscious, and apply cold.

qs.q: When providing first aid, in what position should an unconscious casualty who is breathing and has circulation be placed?
o: On their back, with a roll placed beneath the head.
On their back, with their legs spread apart.
Place the casualty in the recovery position on their side, with the bent knees touching the ground and the upper hand positioned beneath the cheek.
qs.x: An unconscious casualty who is breathing and has circulation goes into the recovery position to keep the airway open.

qs.q: For how long may a tourniquet remain applied to stop bleeding?
o: No more than half an hour in warm weather and no more than one hour in cold weather.
No more than one hour in warm weather and no more than half an hour in cold weather.
There is no limit on how long a tourniquet may remain applied.
qs.x: A tourniquet may stay on up to 1 hour in warm weather and 30 minutes in cold weather, to prevent tissue death.

qs.q: How should you check whether an unconscious casualty is breathing?
o: Hold the casualty’s chin, tilt the head back and observe chest movement for 10 seconds.

Place one hand on the casualty’s forehead and use two fingers of the other hand to lift the chin and tilt the head back. For 10 seconds, check for breathing by trying to feel exhaled air on your cheek and watching for chest movement.
Without tilting the casualty’s head, lean towards their face and check for breathing for 10 seconds by trying to feel exhaled air on your cheek and watching for chest movement.
qs.x: To check breathing, tilt the head back with one hand on the forehead and two fingers lifting the chin, then feel and watch for 10 seconds.

qs.q: What are the main signs of severe arterial bleeding, and what action should be taken first when providing first aid?
o: Dark-coloured blood flows slowly from the wound. Apply a pressure dressing to the wound, noting how long it should remain in place.

Bright-red blood spurts forcefully from the wound in intermittent jets or a fountain-like stream. Apply finger pressure to the injured artery, then place a tourniquet above the wound as close to it as possible, recording the time it was applied.
Blood flows slowly from the wound. Apply a tourniquet below the injury, recording the time it was applied.
qs.x: In arterial bleeding bright red blood spurts: press the artery first, then apply a tourniquet above the wound and note the time.

qs.q: Is it permitted to give medication to a casualty while providing first aid?
qs.x: Giving medication to the injured is prohibited during first aid.

qs.q: How should bleeding caused by injuries to veins or smaller arteries be controlled?
o: Apply a pressure dressing directly over the injury.
Apply a pressure dressing above the wound.
Apply a pressure dressing below the wound.
qs.x: For venous or minor arterial bleeding, apply the pressure bandage directly over the wound.

qs.q: What initial first aid measures should be taken for injuries sustained in a road traffic accident?
o: Wash the wound with water, remove foreign objects from it, apply sterile cotton to the wound and secure it with a bandage.
Put on medical gloves, clean the wound with an alcoholic iodine solution, apply medicinal ointment and cover it with an adhesive dressing.
Put on medical gloves and, without cleaning the wound, cover it with a sterile gauze pad secured at the edges with adhesive tape or a bandage.
qs.x: Put on gloves and cover the wound, without cleaning it, with a sterile gauze pad secured with tape or a bandage.

qs.q: How should first aid be provided for limb fractures if neither splints nor suitable materials for making them are available?
o: Secure the upper limb to the torso with the arm extended along the body. Tie the lower limbs together, placing soft material between them.
Bend the upper limb at the elbow, support it in a sling and secure it to the torso. Tie the lower limbs together, placing soft material between them.
Bend the upper limb at the elbow, support it in a sling and secure it to the torso. Tie the lower limbs together.
qs.x: Without splints, bend the arm at the elbow in a sling and secure it to the torso, and tie the legs together with padding between.

qs.q: Under which circumstances should a person injured in a road traffic accident be removed from the passenger compartment of a vehicle?
o: If there is a high risk of the vehicle overturning, catching fire or exploding, or if the injured person loses consciousness.

If there is a high risk of the vehicle overturning, catching fire or exploding; if the injured person is suffering from hypothermia or has lost consciousness and is not breathing; or if first aid cannot be provided inside the vehicle.
If there is a high risk of the vehicle overturning, catching fire or exploding, or if the injured person has severe bleeding or a traumatic brain injury.
qs.x: Remove the person if there is danger (rollover, fire, explosion), hypothermia, loss of consciousness or breathing, or first aid is impossible inside.

qs.q: When providing first aid for a superficial thermal burn (redness and swelling of the skin, blisters filled with clear fluid at the burn site, and severe pain), what should be done?
o: Pour cold water over the burned area, cover it with a sterile dressing and bandage it tightly.
Burst the blisters, remove clothing remnants from the burned area, cover it with a sterile dressing without bandaging it, apply something cold if possible, and give the injured person water to drink.

Cool the burned area with water for 20 minutes. Without bursting the blisters or removing clothing remnants, cover the burned area with a sterile dressing without bandaging it, apply something cold if possible, and give the injured person water to drink.
qs.x: Cool a superficial burn with water for 20 minutes, do not open blisters, and cover with a sterile pad without bandaging.
